title: After another strong quarter, Target lifts annual sales growth target to 6%
html:
People walk by a Target store in midtown Manhattan, New York, last year.Kylie Cooper/Reuters

Target TGT-N reported its third consecutive strong sales quarter on Wednesday, the latest step in its emergence from a multiyear slump.

The retailer also raised its annual sales growth forecast, betting on resilient holiday shopping demand in categories such as toys and snacks.

Under CEO Michael Fiddelke, who took the reins earlier this year, Target has invested around US$5-billion to freshen its merchandise mix, and on Wednesday said its capital expenditures would total another US$5-billion to US$6-billion in 2027.

So far, the investments have paid off: after four years of declines, Target’s stock has climbed about 60 per cent year to date. That’s in a year marked by steep inflation and record-high fuel prices, spurring U.S. shoppers to be selective on discretionary purchases and trade down on essentials.

Target has remodelled stores and focused on categories like grocery, drawing in customers with in-demand items like protein snacks.

Apparel, home decor still a work in progress

The hardlines category, which consists of toys and electronics, was once again a bright spot, with sales jumping nearly 27 per cent in the quarter. Target has overhauled the business this year by shifting its focus to collectibles and wearable tech from larger products like TVs.

Sales in the food and beverages category rose 6.6 per cent in the three months through October.

But Target has yet to get its groove back in big-ticket, discretionary items like apparel and home decor – two categories that together account for about 30 per cent of the company’s merchandise sales.

Sales were down 3.8 per cent in the apparel business in the reported quarter, while home decor grew 2.5 per cent.

The two categories are the hardest to improve because they hinge on appealing to evolving consumer tastes and persuading shoppers to make discretionary purchases, said RBC Capital Markets analyst Steve Shemesh.

Getting such product lines right “will prove imperative to long-term profitability,” said Morningstar analyst Brett Husslein. “It is crucial.”

Executives, for their part, say the strategy in apparel and home has produced positive results where resources have been expended.

“We tackled bedding, we tackled bath, we tackled kids’ home,” Chief Merchandising Officer Cara Sylvester said in a call with media ahead of results. “Those are areas that are all performing really well.”

Fiddelke said on the same call that “we’ve got momentum in parts of each of those categories, and we need more,” adding, “We haven’t arrived.”

Total comparable sales grew 5.6 per cent in the third quarter that included the back-to-school shopping season, and beat estimates of 3.5 per cent. Traffic was up 5 per cent in the period, while digital comparable sales were up 9.8 per cent.

Target now expects annual net sales growth of around 6 per cent, compared with about 5 per cent expected earlier.

The company projected adjusted earnings per share in the range of US$10.65 to US$11.40, which includes about US$2.14 per share benefit from tariff refunds received so far this year.
summary: CEO Fiddelke’s investments paying off, with the stock up about 60% this year
